content: Yeast infection, commonly known scientifically as candidiasis, is an infection caused primarily by the fungus Candida albicans, which naturally resides on human skin and mucous membranes. It often affects the vaginal area in women but can occur in other body parts including the mouth and skin folds. Mechanistically, yeast overgrowth happens when the normal balance of microorganisms is disrupted by factors such as antibiotic use, hormonal changes, or immune suppression. Symptoms typically include itching, abnormal discharge, redness, and irritation. Yeast infections are significant in women's health due to their high prevalence and impact on quality of life. Synonyms include candidiasis and moniliasis. Evaluation involves history taking, physical exam, and sometimes microscopic examination or culture. Management centers on antifungal medications available as creams, suppositories, or oral tablets. Lifestyle factors like hygiene, clothing choices, and diet may influence risk. Limitations in evidence exist regarding some home remedies and alternative therapies. Safety considerations emphasize correct diagnosis to rule out other infections, avoiding unnecessary antifungal use, and understanding potential side effects. Early treatment generally leads to symptom resolution within days to a week, but recurrent infections require further medical evaluation.

content: A yeast infection is a fungal infection caused primarily by the organism Candida albicans. It commonly affects the vagina but can also occur in the mouth (oral thrush) and skin. Normally, Candida species live harmlessly on skin and mucous membranes, but under certain conditions, they can multiply excessively and cause infection. This imbalance leads to symptoms such as itching, redness, swelling, and discharge. The term candidiasis is the medical term synonymous with yeast infection.

chunk_title: Causes and Mechanisms of Yeast Infections
content: Yeast infections result from an overgrowth of Candida fungi, most often Candida albicans. The fungi are opportunistic organisms that thrive when the natural defense mechanisms of the body are compromised or when normal bacterial flora is disrupted. Common causes include antibiotic use, which reduces protective bacteria; hormonal changes such as those during pregnancy or from birth control pills; diabetes which can increase sugar available to yeast; and immunosuppression. The overgrowth leads to local inflammation and symptoms.

content: Several factors increase the risk of developing yeast infections. These include recent or prolonged antibiotic use, high estrogen levels (pregnancy, hormonal contraceptives), uncontrolled diabetes, immunosuppressive conditions or medications, tight or non-breathable clothing, poor hygiene, and high sugar diets. Women who have recurrent infections may have an underlying predisposing condition. Knowing these risk factors helps in prevention and assessment.

chunk_title: Symptoms and Signs of Yeast Infection
content: The hallmark symptoms of a vaginal yeast infection include intense itching of the vulva and vagina, thick white vaginal discharge often described as 'cottage cheese-like,' redness and swelling of the vulvar area, burning sensation during urination or intercourse, and vaginal discomfort. Symptoms usually develop over a few days. Some also experience irritation without discharge. It is important to differentiate these symptoms from other infections that may require different treatment.

chunk_title: Diagnosis and Evaluation of Yeast Infections
content: Healthcare providers diagnose yeast infections primarily through patient history and physical examination. They may examine the vaginal area and look for characteristic signs. Microscopic examination (wet mount) of vaginal discharge can show yeast cells and pseudohyphae. In uncertain cases, cultures may be done. Proper diagnosis differentiates yeast infections from bacterial vaginosis or sexually transmitted infections, guiding appropriate treatment.

content: Treatment typically involves antifungal medications, which can be topical (creams, ointments, suppositories) or oral (fluconazole tablets). Over-the-counter antifungal treatments are available for uncomplicated cases. Prescription medications may be required for recurrent or severe infections. Treatment duration ranges from 1 to 7 days depending on the preparation and severity. It is important to complete the course and follow medical advice to prevent recurrence.

content: Preventive measures include wearing breathable cotton underwear, avoiding tight-fitting clothes, maintaining good genital hygiene, avoiding unnecessary antibiotic use, and controlling blood sugar in diabetics. Some suggest that dietary modifications reducing sugar intake may help, although evidence is limited. Avoiding douching and scented feminine products is recommended to maintain normal vaginal flora. These lifestyle changes can reduce the frequency and severity of infections.

Pregnant women should consult healthcare providers before using treatment. Persistent or recurrent symptoms warrant medical evaluation to rule out other causes or complications. Understanding treatment side effects and following recommended dosages promote safe management.

chunk_title: Yeast Infection in Men and Other Body Sites
content: Though more common in women, men can also develop yeast infections, typically on the penis, presenting as redness, itching, or rash. Yeast infections can also occur as oral thrush or in skin folds, particularly in immunocompromised individuals. Recognizing these presentations expands understanding beyond vaginal infections and emphasizes the need for appropriate diagnosis and treatment.
